Question: Why should baseball be a circus with pitches clearly balls or strikes and umpires calling the opposite? Is the umpire union so strong that they can’t incorporate electronic calls?
Answer: It’s not the umpires union. In fact, I don’t think they’d have grounds to complain if MLB just said “we’re doing this” because it wouldn’t affect the number of jobs for umpires or their working conditions. It’s much more the basic conservatism of MLB (meaning the people running the league from the commissioner on down, including a fair number of umpires, players, and managers). They know a significant amount of the fan base will accept “we’ve always done it this way” as an excuse for not doing something, and they’re not quite yet convinced that there are enough fans who have had enough of poor ball/strike umpiring to really want to see a change.

Name: Mike Jones
Question: In baseball, what determines the shape of the home plate? It could have been a rectangle or a circle, but rather it is sort of a diamond shape.
Answer: Before 1899, home plate was round. It could be pretty much any round object of approximately the right size. In 1899 (or possibly 1900), the rules changed requiring home plate to be a 12″ or 16″ square sitting in the point created by the foul lines with one point toward the catcher and one toward the pitcher. The plate was generally made of some hard surface, possibly stone. Sliding into home was understandably un-popular at that point. In 1901, the change to the familiar five-sided “house” was made as well as having the plate made of rubber. Today, here’s what Rule 2.02 says: Home base shall be marked by a five-sided slab of whitened rubber. It shall be a 17-inch square with two of the corners removed so that one edge is 17 inches long, two adjacent sides are 8½ inches and the remaining two sides are 12 inches and set at an angle to make a point. It shall be set in the ground with the point at the intersection of the lines extending from home base to first base and to third base; with the 17-inch edge facing the pitcher’s plate, and the two 12-inch edges coinciding with the first and third base lines. The top edges of home base shall be beveled and the base shall be fixed in the ground level with the ground surface. They even provide a helpful diagram: None of this explains why the change, though. And the answer is pretty simple: extending the “side” points toward the pitcher makes it easier for the umpire to determine the strike zone. With the old scheme, you could have a pitch (particularly a curve ball) that would go through the strike zone and never actually be over the plate (trajectory exaggerated for effect): Even a straight pitch thrown from one end of the rubber or the other could do that.
